# Welcome {.unnumbered}

::: {.lead}
This is a summary report and walkthrough of my capstone project at **Western Governors University**.
:::

<br>

[![Photo by David Eluwole from Pexels](./images/david-eluwole.jpg "Group of African women")](https://www.pexels.com/photo/line-of-standing-woman-with-afro-hairstyle-18236930/){target="_blank"}

<br>

### Research Question

::: {.lead appearance="simple"}
**"Among female homicide victims, can weather conditions, agency population, and location predict whether the victim is Black or not Black?"**
:::

---

<br>

### Why I Asked It

Other studies have linked hot weather to more violent crime, but these relationships haven't been studied among female homicide victims.

<br>

### Scope

::: {.card style="border-top: none;"}
- 15,766 records of female homicide victims whose race is known, from 2017 through 2020, across all 50 states and D.C.
- Four public sources: homicide records from the Murder Accountability Project, agency populations from DataLumos, daily weather from the Open-Meteo weather API, and state coordinates from Kaggle
- Associations only: the project doesn't claim that weather or agency size causes differences in victim race
:::

<br>

### How It Was Built

I followed the CRoss-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) and did the work in R, in Positron, across three Quarto notebooks: the first cleans and merges the raw data, the second explores it, and the third builds and evaluates the model.

<br>

### What's Included

::: {.card style="border-top: none; border-left: none;"}
`Cleaning`
: merging the homicide, agency, and weather data

`Analysis`
: exploring the outcome and the predictors

`Modeling`
: logistic regression, evaluation, and practical significance

`References`
: the sources cited in the scripts
:::
